import FormalConjectures.Millenium.NavierStokes

/-!
# Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations

The incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for a velocity field $u(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^3$
and a pressure $p(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}$ are
$$\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0.$$

Wikipedia lists "Regularity of solutions of Euler equations" as an unsolved problem: whether
solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations can form a singularity in finite
time. We follow the precise formulation of Elgindi (Question 1.1 of
[arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)): can a smooth, finite-energy solution
$u$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,T)$ satisfy $\lim_{t \to T} \sup_x |\nabla u(x,t)| = +\infty$?
We also state Elgindi's main theorem, which answers the analogous question positively for the
lower regularity class $C^{1,\alpha}$.

## Conventions

The velocity is `u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³` and the pressure is `p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ`, so that `u x t`
is the velocity at position `x` and time `t`, as in `FormalConjectures.Millenium.NavierStokes`,
from which we reuse the divergence `∇⬝`. Solutions live on the time interval `Ico 0 T`, and
the time derivative is `derivWithin` relative to `Ico 0 T`, which is one-sided at `t = 0`.
The term $(u \cdot \nabla) u$ is the spatial derivative of `u` applied to `u`.

We consider the free equations (no external force), as in the Wikipedia article. Elgindi's
question also allows a force $f \in (C^\infty \cap L^2)(\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,T])$; without
uniform bounds on $f$ this makes the question degenerate, since a locally finite family of
rescaled compactly supported steady solutions switched on by such a force develops an unbounded
gradient as $t \to T$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Euler equations (fluid dynamics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- T. M. Elgindi, *Finite-time singularity formation for $C^{1,\alpha}$ solutions to the
  incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$*, Ann. of Math. (2) 194 (2021), 647–727.
  [arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)
-/

blocks.name: IsOdd
blocks.text:
/-- A vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is **odd** (in the sense of Elgindi,
Definition 1.2) if for each $i$ the component $v_i$ is odd in the variable $x_i$ and even in the
other two variables. Here `x - (2 * x j) • EuclideanSpace.single j 1` is the reflection of `x`
that changes the sign of the `j`-th coordinate. -/
def IsOdd (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∀ (x : ℝ³) (i j : Fin 3),
    v (x - (2 * x j) • EuclideanSpace.single j 1) i = if i = j then -v x i else v x i

  ContDiff ℝ 1 v ∧ (∀ x, ‖fderiv ℝ v x‖ ≤ C) ∧ HolderWith C α (fderiv ℝ v)
blocks.docstring:
A vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ with constant
`C` if it is continuously differentiable and its derivative $\nabla v$ is bounded by `C` and
$\alpha$-Hölder continuous with constant `C`. Following Elgindi (Section 1.5), no bound on `v`

structure IsEulerSolution (T : ℝ) (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- The Euler momentum equation $\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p = 0$. -/
  euler : ∀ x, ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T,
    derivWithin (u x ·) (Ico 0 T) t + fderiv ℝ (u · t) x (u x t) + gradient (p · t) x = 0
  /-- The incompressibility constraint $\nabla \cdot u = 0$. -/
  div_free : ∀ x, ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, ∇⬝ (u · t) x = 0

structure IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution (T : ℝ) (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ) :
    Prop extends IsEulerSolution T u p where
  /-- The velocity is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$. -/
  velocity_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (↿u) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)
  /-- The pressure is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$. -/
  pressure_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (↿p) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)
  /-- The velocity is square-integrable at each time $t \in [0, T)$ (finite energy). -/
  memLp : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, MemLp (u · t) 2
  /-- The kinetic energy is conserved: $\int |u(x,t)|^2 \, dx = \int |u(x,0)|^2 \, dx$
  for all $t \in [0, T)$. -/
  energy_conservation : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, ∫ x, ‖u x t‖ ^ 2 = ∫ x, ‖u x 0‖ ^ 2
  /-- The gradient of the velocity is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^3$ at each time $t \in [0, T)$. -/
  gradient_bounded : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, BddAbove (range fun x => ‖fderiv ℝ (u · t) x‖)
blocks.docstring:
A smooth, finite-energy solution `(u, p)` of the incompressible Euler equations on
$\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$, in the sense of Question 1.1 of Elgindi's paper (with $f = 0$):
- `u` and `p` are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$;
- `u` has finite kinetic energy, $u(\cdot, t) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for every $t \in [0, T)$;
- the energy balance $\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |u(x,t)|^2 \, dx = 0$ holds, which we
  state in integrated form as conservation of energy;
- for each time $t < T$, the gradient $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^3$, so
  that the solution is regular before time $T$ and a blow-up of $\sup_x |\nabla u(x,t)|$ as
  $t \to T$ is a genuine loss of regularity at time $T$. Without this condition a locally
  finite superposition of rescaled compactly supported steady solutions, which has an unbounded
  gradient at every time, would count as a singular solution.

justification.name: EulerEquations.IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution
justification.why_needed: Elgindi's Question 1.1 solution class: C^∞ velocity and pressure, finite energy, energy conservation, bounded gradient before T.

blocks.docstring:
**Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations** (Wikipedia list entry), in the precise
form of Question 1.1 of Elgindi's paper, for the free equations ($f = 0$):

Is it possible that a $C^\infty$, divergence-free, finite-energy solution $u$ of the
three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$, satisfying the
energy balance and with $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ bounded for each $t < T$, has
$$\lim_{t \to T} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^3} |\nabla u(x,t)| = +\infty?$$

Here $|\nabla u(x,t)|$ is the operator norm of the spatial derivative `fderiv ℝ (u · t) x`.
A positive answer means finite-time singularity formation for smooth solutions; a negative
answer means global regularity.

/-- **Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations** (Wikipedia list entry), in the precise
form of Question 1.1 of Elgindi's paper, for the free equations ($f = 0$):

Is it possible that a $C^\infty$, divergence-free, finite-energy solution $u$ of the
three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$, satisfying the
energy balance and with $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ bounded for each $t < T$, has
$$\lim_{t \to T} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^3} |\nabla u(x,t)| = +\infty?$$

Here $|\nabla u(x,t)|$ is the operator norm of the spatial derivative `fderiv ℝ (u · t) x`.
A positive answer means finite-time singularity formation for smooth solutions; a negative
answer means global regularity. -/

theorem euler_equations :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ T > 0, ∃ (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ),
      IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution T u p ∧
        Tendsto (fun t => ⨆ x, ‖fderiv ℝ (u · t) x‖) (𝓝[<] T) atTop := by
  sorry

**Elgindi's theorem** (Main Theorem of [arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)):
finite-time singularity formation for $C^{1,\alpha}$ solutions of the three-dimensional
incompressible Euler equations.

There exist $\alpha > 0$ and a divergence-free, odd initial velocity
$u_0 \in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ whose vorticity $\omega_0 = \nabla \times u_0$ satisfies
$|\omega_0(x)| \le C / (|x|^\alpha + 1)$ for some constant $C > 0$, such that the (unique)
odd classical solution of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, 1)$ with initial
velocity $u_0$ and no external force satisfies
$$\lim_{t \to 1} \int_0^t \|\omega(\cdot, s)\|_{L^\infty} \, ds = +\infty,$$
where $\omega = \nabla \times u$ is the vorticity of the solution. The integral is taken in
$[0, \infty]$, and $\|\omega(\cdot, s)\|_{L^\infty} = \sup_x |\omega(x, s)|$.

This is stated as the existence of such a blowing-up odd classical solution; the uniqueness
of the solution, which Elgindi's statement takes from the classical local well-posedness
theory, is not asserted. This is a special case of the blow-up question `euler_equations` with
the regularity $C^\infty$ replaced by $C^{1,\alpha}$; the solutions have infinite energy and do
not satisfy the energy balance, so the question for smooth finite-energy solutions remains
open.

In fluid dynamics, the Euler equations are a set of partial differential equations governing adiabatic and inviscid flow. They are named after Leonhard Euler. In particular, they correspond to the Navier–Stokes equations with zero viscosity and zero thermal conductivity.
The Euler equations can be applied to incompressible and compressible flows. The incompressible Euler equations consist of Cauchy equations for conservation of mass and balance of momentum, together with the incompressibility condition that the flow velocity is  divergence-free. The compressible Euler equations consist of equations for conservation of mass, balance of momentum, and balance of energy, together with a suitable constitutive equation for the specific energy density of the fluid. Historically, only the equations of conservation of mass and balance of momentum were derived by Euler. However, fluid dynamics literature often refers to the full set of the compressible Euler equations – including the energy equation – as "the compressible Euler equations".
The mathematical characters of the incompressible and compressible Euler equations are rather different. For constant fluid density, the incompressible equations can be written as a quasilinear advection equation for the fluid velocity together with an elliptic Poisson's equation for the pressure. On the other hand, the compressible Euler equations form a quasilinear hyperbolic system of conservation equations.

import FormalConjectures.Millenium.NavierStokes

/-!
# Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations

The incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for a velocity field $u(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^3$
and a pressure $p(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}$ are
$$\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0.$$

Wikipedia lists "Regularity of solutions of Euler equations" as an unsolved problem: whether
solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations can form a singularity in finite
time. We follow the precise formulation of Elgindi (Question 1.1 of
[arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)): can a smooth, finite-energy solution
$u$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,T)$ satisfy $\lim_{t \to T} \sup_x |\nabla u(x,t)| = +\infty$?
We also state Elgindi's main theorem, which answers the analogous question positively for the
lower regularity class $C^{1,\alpha}$.

## Conventions

The velocity is `u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³` and the pressure is `p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ`, so that `u x t`
is the velocity at position `x` and time `t`, as in `FormalConjectures.Millenium.NavierStokes`,
from which we reuse the divergence `∇⬝`. Solutions live on the time interval `Ico 0 T`, and
the time derivative is `derivWithin` relative to `Ico 0 T`, which is one-sided at `t = 0`.
The term $(u \cdot \nabla) u$ is the spatial derivative of `u` applied to `u`.

We consider the free equations (no external force), as in the Wikipedia article. Elgindi's
question also allows a force $f \in (C^\infty \cap L^2)(\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0,T])$; without
uniform bounds on $f$ this makes the question degenerate, since a locally finite family of
rescaled compactly supported steady solutions switched on by such a force develops an unbounded
gradient as $t \to T$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Euler equations (fluid dynamics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- T. M. Elgindi, *Finite-time singularity formation for $C^{1,\alpha}$ solutions to the
  incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$*, Ann. of Math. (2) 194 (2021), 647–727.
  [arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)
-/

/-- The curl $\nabla \times v$ of a vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ at a
point $x$, with components $\partial_2 v_3 - \partial_3 v_2$, $\partial_3 v_1 - \partial_1 v_3$
and $\partial_1 v_2 - \partial_2 v_1$. Here $\partial_j v_i$ is the `i`-th component of
`fderiv ℝ v x` applied to the `j`-th standard basis vector. The curl of the velocity field of a
fluid is its vorticity.
If `v` is not differentiable at `x`, then `fderiv` is the zero map and the curl is `0`. -/
noncomputable def curl (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (x : ℝ³) : ℝ³ :=
  let D : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℝ := fun j i => fderiv ℝ v x (EuclideanSpace.single j 1) i
  !₂[D 1 2 - D 2 1, D 2 0 - D 0 2, D 0 1 - D 1 0]

/-- The curl of the zero vector field is zero. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem curl_zero (x : ℝ³) : curl 0 x = 0 := by
  simp [curl]

/-- The curl of a constant vector field is zero. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem curl_const (c x : ℝ³) : curl (fun _ => c) x = 0 := by
  simp [curl]

/-- The curl is `0` at points where `fderiv` has its junk value. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem curl_of_not_differentiableAt {v : ℝ³ → ℝ³} {x : ℝ³}
    (hv : ¬ DifferentiableAt ℝ v x) : curl v x = 0 := by
  simp [curl, fderiv_zero_of_not_differentiableAt hv]

/-- The shear flow $v(x) = (x_2, 0, 0)$ has constant vorticity $\nabla \times v = (0, 0, -1)$. -/
@[category test, AMS 35]
theorem curl_shear (x : ℝ³) :
    curl (fun y => (EuclideanSpace.proj (1 : Fin 3)).smulRight (EuclideanSpace.single 0 1 : ℝ³) y)
      x = !₂[0, 0, -1] := by
  simp only [curl, ContinuousLinearMap.fderiv]
  simp [EuclideanSpace.single_apply]

/-- A vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is **odd** (in the sense of Elgindi,
Definition 1.2) if for each $i$ the component $v_i$ is odd in the variable $x_i$ and even in the
other two variables. Here `x - (2 * x j) • EuclideanSpace.single j 1` is the reflection of `x`
that changes the sign of the `j`-th coordinate. -/
def IsOdd (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∀ (x : ℝ³) (i j : Fin 3),
    v (x - (2 * x j) • EuclideanSpace.single j 1) i = if i = j then -v x i else v x i

/-- The zero vector field is odd. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem isOdd_zero : IsOdd 0 := by
  intro x i j
  simp

/-- The identity vector field $x \mapsto x$ is odd. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem isOdd_id : IsOdd id := by
  intro x i j
  by_cases h : i = j
  · subst h
    simp
    ring
  · simp [h, EuclideanSpace.single_apply]

/-- A non-zero constant vector field is not odd. -/
@[category test, AMS 35]
theorem not_isOdd_const {c : ℝ³} (hc : c ≠ 0) : ¬ IsOdd (fun _ => c) := by
  intro h
  apply hc
  ext i
  have := h 0 i i
  simp only [if_true] at this
  simp only [WithLp.ofLp_zero, Pi.zero_apply]
  linarith

/-- A vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ with constant
`C` if it is continuously differentiable and its derivative $\nabla v$ is bounded by `C` and
$\alpha$-Hölder continuous with constant `C`. Following Elgindi (Section 1.5), no bound on `v`
itself is imposed, so `v` may be unbounded. -/
def IsC1HolderWith (C α : ℝ≥0) (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ContDiff ℝ 1 v ∧ (∀ x, ‖fderiv ℝ v x‖ ≤ C) ∧ HolderWith C α (fderiv ℝ v)

/-- A vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ if it is
continuously differentiable and its derivative $\nabla v$ is bounded and $\alpha$-Hölder
continuous. -/
def IsC1Holder (α : ℝ≥0) (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ C, IsC1HolderWith C α v

/-- A constant vector field is of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ with constant `0` for every $\alpha$. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem isC1HolderWith_const (α : ℝ≥0) (c : ℝ³) : IsC1HolderWith 0 α (fun _ => c) :=
  ⟨contDiff_const, fun x => by simp, fun x y => by simp⟩

/-- A constant vector field is of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ for every $\alpha$. -/
@[category API, AMS 35]
theorem isC1Holder_const (α : ℝ≥0) (c : ℝ³) : IsC1Holder α (fun _ => c) :=
  ⟨0, isC1HolderWith_const α c⟩

/-- A pair `(u, p)` of a velocity field and a pressure solves the incompressible Euler equations
without external force on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$:
$$\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0.$$
The time derivative is taken within `Ico 0 T`, so it is one-sided at `t = 0`. -/
structure IsEulerSolution (T : ℝ) (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- The Euler momentum equation $\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p = 0$. -/
  euler : ∀ x, ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T,
    derivWithin (u x ·) (Ico 0 T) t + fderiv ℝ (u · t) x (u x t) + gradient (p · t) x = 0
  /-- The incompressibility constraint $\nabla \cdot u = 0$. -/
  div_free : ∀ x, ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, ∇⬝ (u · t) x = 0

/-- The fluid at rest solves the Euler equations. -/
@[category test, AMS 35]
theorem isEulerSolution_zero (T : ℝ) : IsEulerSolution T 0 0 where
  euler x t _ := by simp
  div_free x t _ := by simp

/-- A smooth, finite-energy solution `(u, p)` of the incompressible Euler equations on
$\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$, in the sense of Question 1.1 of Elgindi's paper (with $f = 0$):
- `u` and `p` are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$;
- `u` has finite kinetic energy, $u(\cdot, t) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for every $t \in [0, T)$;
- the energy balance $\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |u(x,t)|^2 \, dx = 0$ holds, which we
  state in integrated form as conservation of energy;
- for each time $t < T$, the gradient $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^3$, so
  that the solution is regular before time $T$ and a blow-up of $\sup_x |\nabla u(x,t)|$ as
  $t \to T$ is a genuine loss of regularity at time $T$. Without this condition a locally
  finite superposition of rescaled compactly supported steady solutions, which has an unbounded
  gradient at every time, would count as a singular solution. -/
structure IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution (T : ℝ) (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ) :
    Prop extends IsEulerSolution T u p where
  /-- The velocity is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$. -/
  velocity_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (↿u) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)
  /-- The pressure is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$. -/
  pressure_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (↿p) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)
  /-- The velocity is square-integrable at each time $t \in [0, T)$ (finite energy). -/
  memLp : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, MemLp (u · t) 2
  /-- The kinetic energy is conserved: $\int |u(x,t)|^2 \, dx = \int |u(x,0)|^2 \, dx$
  for all $t \in [0, T)$. -/
  energy_conservation : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, ∫ x, ‖u x t‖ ^ 2 = ∫ x, ‖u x 0‖ ^ 2
  /-- The gradient of the velocity is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^3$ at each time $t \in [0, T)$. -/
  gradient_bounded : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, BddAbove (range fun x => ‖fderiv ℝ (u · t) x‖)

/-- The fluid at rest is a smooth finite-energy solution of the Euler equations. -/
@[category test, AMS 35]
theorem isSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution_zero (T : ℝ) :
    IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution T 0 0 where
  toIsEulerSolution := isEulerSolution_zero T
  velocity_smooth := contDiffOn_const
  pressure_smooth := contDiffOn_const
  memLp t _ := by simp
  energy_conservation t _ := by simp
  gradient_bounded t _ := ⟨0, by rintro _ ⟨x, rfl⟩; simp⟩

/-- **Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations** (Wikipedia list entry), in the precise
form of Question 1.1 of Elgindi's paper, for the free equations ($f = 0$):

Is it possible that a $C^\infty$, divergence-free, finite-energy solution $u$ of the
three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$, satisfying the
energy balance and with $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ bounded for each $t < T$, has
$$\lim_{t \to T} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^3} |\nabla u(x,t)| = +\infty?$$

Here $|\nabla u(x,t)|$ is the operator norm of the spatial derivative `fderiv ℝ (u · t) x`.
A positive answer means finite-time singularity formation for smooth solutions; a negative
answer means global regularity. -/
@[category research open, AMS 35 76]
theorem euler_equations :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ T > 0, ∃ (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ),
      IsSmoothFiniteEnergyEulerSolution T u p ∧
        Tendsto (fun t => ⨆ x, ‖fderiv ℝ (u · t) x‖) (𝓝[<] T) atTop := by
  sorry

/-- A classical solution `(u, p)` of the incompressible Euler equations on
$\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$ of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ with initial velocity `u₀`:
- `u` is $C^1$ in space and time on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$ with `u x 0 = u₀ x`;
- on each time interval $[0, T']$ with $T' < T$, the spatial derivative $\nabla u(\cdot, t)$ is
  bounded and $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, uniformly in $t \in [0, T']$;
- the pressure $p(\cdot, t)$ is $C^1$ in space for every $t \in [0, T)$.

The velocity itself is not required to be bounded, since the solutions of Elgindi's theorem
grow at spatial infinity and have infinite energy. -/
structure IsClassicalEulerSolution (α : ℝ≥0) (T : ℝ) (u₀ : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³)
    (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop extends IsEulerSolution T u p where
  /-- The initial condition $u(x, 0) = u_0(x)$. -/
  initial_condition : ∀ x, u x 0 = u₀ x
  /-- The velocity is $C^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T)$. -/
  velocity_contDiff : ContDiffOn ℝ 1 (↿u) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)
  /-- The velocity is uniformly of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ in space on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, T']$
  for every $T' < T$. -/
  velocity_holder : ∀ T' < T, ∃ C, ∀ t ∈ Icc 0 T', IsC1HolderWith C α (u · t)
  /-- The pressure is $C^1$ in space at each time $t \in [0, T)$. -/
  pressure_contDiff : ∀ t ∈ Ico 0 T, ContDiff ℝ 1 (p · t)

/-- The fluid at rest is a classical solution of the Euler equations with zero initial velocity. -/
@[category test, AMS 35]
theorem isClassicalEulerSolution_zero (α : ℝ≥0) (T : ℝ) : IsClassicalEulerSolution α T 0 0 0 where
  toIsEulerSolution := isEulerSolution_zero T
  initial_condition _ := rfl
  velocity_contDiff := contDiffOn_const
  velocity_holder _ _ := ⟨0, fun _ _ => isC1HolderWith_const α 0⟩
  pressure_contDiff _ _ := contDiff_const

/-- **Elgindi's theorem** (Main Theorem of [arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)):
finite-time singularity formation for $C^{1,\alpha}$ solutions of the three-dimensional
incompressible Euler equations.

There exist $\alpha > 0$ and a divergence-free, odd initial velocity
$u_0 \in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ whose vorticity $\omega_0 = \nabla \times u_0$ satisfies
$|\omega_0(x)| \le C / (|x|^\alpha + 1)$ for some constant $C > 0$, such that the (unique)
odd classical solution of class $C^{1,\alpha}$ on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, 1)$ with initial
velocity $u_0$ and no external force satisfies
$$\lim_{t \to 1} \int_0^t \|\omega(\cdot, s)\|_{L^\infty} \, ds = +\infty,$$
where $\omega = \nabla \times u$ is the vorticity of the solution. The integral is taken in
$[0, \infty]$, and $\|\omega(\cdot, s)\|_{L^\infty} = \sup_x |\omega(x, s)|$.

This is stated as the existence of such a blowing-up odd classical solution; the uniqueness
of the solution, which Elgindi's statement takes from the classical local well-posedness
theory, is not asserted. This is a special case of the blow-up question `euler_equations` with
the regularity $C^\infty$ replaced by $C^{1,\alpha}$; the solutions have infinite energy and do
not satisfy the energy balance, so the question for smooth finite-energy solutions remains
open. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 35 76]
theorem euler_equations.variants.elgindi :
    ∃ α : ℝ≥0, 0 < α ∧ ∃ u₀ : ℝ³ → ℝ³,
      IsC1Holder α u₀ ∧ (∀ x, ∇⬝ u₀ x = 0) ∧ IsOdd u₀ ∧
      (∃ C > 0, ∀ x, ‖curl u₀ x‖ ≤ C / (‖x‖ ^ (α : ℝ) + 1)) ∧
      ∃ (u : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ³) (p : ℝ³ → ℝ → ℝ),
        IsClassicalEulerSolution α 1 u₀ u p ∧ (∀ t ∈ Ico (0 : ℝ) 1, IsOdd (u · t)) ∧
        Tendsto (fun t => ∫⁻ s in Ioc 0 t, ⨆ x, (‖curl (u · s) x‖₊ : ℝ≥0∞)) (𝓝[<] 1) (𝓝 ⊤) := by
  sorry

end EulerEquations

items: Domain and forcing (slot 1): the problem is set on ℝ³ (Elgindi; Wikipedia's 'three-dimensional') for the free equations f ≡ 0, as in the Wikipedia article's 'free equations' convention. Elgindi's Question 1.1 allows f ∈ (C^∞ ∩ L²)(ℝ³×[0,T]); I did not include this because, with only those conditions on f, the literal question is degenerate: turning on (with smooth time cut-offs) infinitely many rescaled copies λ_k V((x−x_k)/μ_k) of Gavrilov's compactly supported smooth steady Euler solution V, placed at x_k → ∞ with μ_k = 2^{-k}, gives a C^∞ finite-energy solution satisfying the energy balance with a forcing that is C^∞ ∩ L² on ℝ³×[0,T] and sup_x|∇u(x,t)| → ∞ as t → T. Including f would require inventing uniform decay hypotheses (à la Fefferman) that are not in either source. The f ≡ 0 question is the standard open problem and is the case Elgindi's Main Theorem treats.

Added hypothesis (slot 1): gradient_bounded requires sup_x ‖∇u(x,t)‖ < ∞ for each t < T. Without it the statement is trivially answered 'yes' by the stationary, locally finite superposition of rescaled Gavrilov steady states (smooth, finite conserved energy, sup_x|∇u| = ∞ for all t). This is the implicit content of 'regular before T, singular at T' (BKM framing) and is explained in the structure docstring.

Energy hypotheses (slot 1): 'finite energy' is MemLp (u · t) 2 volume for each t ∈ [0,T); Elgindi's energy balance d/dt ∫|u|² = 2∫u·f with f = 0 is stated in integrated form as ∫‖u(x,t)‖² dx = ∫‖u(x,0)‖² dx, avoiding differentiability of the energy in t.

Smoothness (slot 1): both u and p are required to be C^∞ on ℝ³×[0,T) jointly (ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (↿u) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 T)); requiring p smooth avoids the junk value gradient = 0 at points of non-differentiability of p. A genuine smooth solution always has a jointly smooth pressure (∇p = −∂_t u − (u·∇)u, normalise p(0,t) = 0).

Blow-up (slot 1): lim_{t→T} sup_x|∇u(x,t)| = +∞ is Tendsto (fun t => ⨆ x, ‖fderiv ℝ (u · t) x‖) (𝓝[<] T) atTop with a real-valued iSup; this is legitimate because gradient_bounded makes the iSup a genuine supremum for t < T. |∇u| is the operator norm of fderiv (any equivalent norm gives the same statement).

Time derivative: derivWithin (u x ·) (Ico 0 T) t, one-sided at t = 0, as in the repository's Millennium NavierStokes file (which uses Ici 0); (u·∇)u is fderiv ℝ (u · t) x (u x t); divergence is the trace of fderiv (junk 0 when not differentiable, harmless under the smoothness hypotheses).

Slot 2 class: Elgindi's 'C^{1,α}_{x,t}([0,1)×ℝ³)' cannot mean globally bounded space-time derivatives (his solution has velocity growing like |x|^{1−α} and unbounded ∂_t u). I interpret it as: u jointly C¹ on ℝ³×[0,1), and for every T' < 1 there is C with ‖∇u(·,t)‖ ≤ C and ∇u(·,t) α-Hölder with constant C for all t ∈ [0,T'] (uniform-in-time spatial C^{1,α}); p(·,t) is C¹ in x. u₀ ∈ C^{1,α}(ℝ³) means C¹ with bounded α-Hölder gradient, with no bound on u₀ itself (Elgindi's notation section; his data have infinite energy).

Slot 2 uniqueness: the theorem speaks of 'the unique local odd solution'. I state the ∃-form (there is an odd classical solution in the class with that data which blows up) and do not assert uniqueness, which is background local well-posedness theory rather than the theorem's content. Oddness is required at every time t ∈ [0,1) (this excludes cheap linear-velocity witnesses u = A(t)x).

Slot 2 blow-up: lim_{t→1} ∫₀ᵗ|ω(s)|_{L^∞} ds = +∞ is Tendsto (fun t => ∫ s in 0..t, ⨆ x, ‖curl (u · s) x‖) (𝓝[<] 1) atTop; the integrand is bounded on [0,t] for t < 1 by the class hypothesis (‖curl‖ ≤ const·‖∇u‖) and lower semicontinuous, so the interval integral is genuine. Vorticity uses the Euclidean norm; the decay bound is ‖curl u₀ x‖ ≤ C/(‖x‖^α + 1) with C : ℝ, C > 0.

Slot 2 exponent: α : ℝ≥0 with 0 < α and no upper bound, matching 'there exists α > 0'. Exponents α > 1 produce no cheap witnesses (Hölder gradient with exponent > 1 forces affine u, oddness forces diagonal linear u, hence ω ≡ 0 and no blow-up).

Odd symmetry (Elgindi Definition 1.2) is encoded via the coordinate reflection x ↦ x − (2 x_j) e_j: v (reflect_j x) i = if i = j then −v x i else v x i; tested on the identity field (odd) and on non-zero constants (not odd). The curl index/sign convention is tested on the shear flow (x₂,0,0) ↦ vorticity (0,0,−1).

reviewer_notes: Source is a bare list entry; made precise via the Wikipedia article ('finite-time singularity formation for 3D incompressible Euler') and Elgindi's Question 1.1. Conventions fixed: domain ℝ³, free equations (f ≡ 0), finite energy (u(·,t) ∈ L²) with energy conservation, u and p C^∞ on ℝ³×[0,T), sup|∇u(·,t)| finite for t<T, blow-up = sup → +∞ as t→T⁻. Reasons f ≡ 0 was chosen over Elgindi's literal forcing class: taken literally the forced question is degenerate (see per-slot), and Elgindi's own Remark shows he treats forcing regularity as decisive; c04's objection on this point is correct. c03's reading (uniformly bounded derivatives of f) is defensible but adds hypotheses absent from every source, so it was not used. The Elgindi variant is stated existentially (a blowing-up odd C^{1,α} classical solution exists for the constructed data) rather than with a uniqueness clause; the docstring records this. α has no upper bound (paper: 'there exists α>0'); c06's added α<1 would strengthen the claim. Both slots compile with only 'declaration uses sorry' warnings. Module docstring says the file reuses `∇⬝` from FormalConjectures.Millenium.NavierStokes (cross-import precedent: Wikipedia/ArtinPrimitiveRootsConjecture imports Millenium.RiemannHypothesis). Residual uncertainty: the interpretive latitude in turning a 5-word list entry into a precise statement (choice f ≡ 0 vs. some forced class; per-time vs. locally-uniform gradient bound) and the mild weakening of 'the unique solution' to an existence claim.
